stimuli.text: Researchers investigated whether caffeine improves attention. They recruited 80 university students and randomly assigned each one to one of two conditions. Participants in one condition drank coffee containing 200 milligrams of caffeine. Participants in the other condition drank decaffeinated coffee that tasted the same. The researchers then recorded the number of targets that each participant correctly detected in a ten-minute computer task.

Researchers investigated whether a night without sleep slows reaction time. They recruited 60 adult volunteers and randomly assigned each one to one of two conditions. Participants in one condition stayed awake all night in the laboratory. Participants in the other condition slept for eight hours in the laboratory. The researchers then recorded the average time in milliseconds that each participant took to press a button when a light appeared.

Researchers investigated whether agreeing to a small request makes people more likely to agree to a large one. They recruited 120 homeowners and randomly assigned each one to one of two conditions. Homeowners in one condition were first asked to sign a road-safety petition and two weeks later were asked to put a large sign in their garden. Homeowners in the other condition were only asked to put the large sign in their garden. The researchers then recorded the percentage of homeowners in each group who agreed to display the sign.

Researchers collected data from 400 high school students. For each one, they recorded the average number of hours slept per night and grade point average. The correlation between the two measures was r = +0.45.

Researchers investigated whether guided hints help children learn to solve puzzles. They recruited 64 five-year-old children and randomly assigned each one to one of two conditions. Children in one condition solved practice puzzles with hints from an adult that were gradually reduced. Children in the other condition solved the same practice puzzles alone. The researchers then recorded the number of new puzzles out of ten that each child later solved without help.

Researchers investigated whether keeping a gratitude journal raises well-being. They recruited 110 adult volunteers and randomly assigned each one to one of two conditions. Participants in one condition wrote down three things they were grateful for every night for a month. Participants in the other condition wrote down three things they had done every night for a month. The researchers then recorded each participant's rating of life satisfaction on a scale from 1 to 10 at the end of the month.

Researchers investigated whether practice quizzes improve memory more than rereading. They recruited 120 university students and randomly assigned each one to one of two conditions. Participants in one condition read a passage once and then took three practice quizzes on it. Participants in the other condition read the same passage four times. The researchers then recorded the percentage of questions that each participant answered correctly on a test one week later.

Researchers investigated whether nausea after a new taste produces an aversion to that taste. They recruited 40 laboratory rats and randomly assigned each one to one of two conditions. Rats in one condition drank sweetened water and were then given an injection that causes mild nausea. Rats in the other condition drank sweetened water and were then given a harmless salt-water injection. The researchers then recorded the volume in milliliters of sweetened water that each rat drank the next day.

Researchers collected data from 1,000 students. For each one, they recorded intelligence test score at age 11 and average school grade at age 16. The correlation between the two measures was r = +0.60.

Researchers investigated whether praise increases hand raising in class. They recruited 50 second-grade students and randomly assigned each one to one of two conditions. Children in one condition were praised by the teacher each time they raised a hand before speaking. Children in the other condition received no special response when they raised a hand. The researchers then recorded the number of times that each child raised a hand during one week.

Researchers investigated whether a new drug reduces anxiety. They recruited 150 adults diagnosed with generalized anxiety disorder and randomly assigned each one to one of two conditions. Participants in one condition took the new drug every day for eight weeks. Participants in the other condition took a placebo pill that looked identical every day for eight weeks. The researchers then recorded each participant's score on a standard anxiety questionnaire after eight weeks.

Researchers investigated whether an expected reward reduces children's later interest in drawing. They recruited 60 preschool children who enjoyed drawing and randomly assigned each one to one of two conditions. Children in one condition were promised a certificate for drawing and received it. Children in the other condition drew with no reward mentioned. The researchers then recorded the number of minutes that each child chose to spend drawing during free time one week later.

Researchers collected data from 300 families. For each one, they recorded the warmth of parenting, as rated by observers and the child's self-esteem score. The correlation between the two measures was r = +0.48.
Researchers collected data from 250 adults. For each one, they recorded resting heart rate and self-rated anxiety. The correlation between the two measures was r = +0.38.

Researchers collected data from 600 university students. For each one, they recorded conscientiousness score on a personality inventory and grade point average. The correlation between the two measures was r = +0.35.

Researchers investigated whether the presence of other people slows the reporting of an emergency. They recruited 80 university students and randomly assigned each one to one of two conditions. Participants in one condition were filling in a form in a room with four other people when smoke began to enter the room. Participants in the other condition were filling in the form alone when smoke began to enter the room. The researchers then recorded the time in seconds before each participant left the room to report the smoke.

Researchers investigated whether regular aerobic exercise improves memory in older adults. They recruited 100 adults aged 60 to 75 and randomly assigned each one to one of two conditions. Participants in one condition walked briskly for 40 minutes three times a week for six months. Participants in the other condition did gentle stretching for the same amount of time. The researchers then recorded the number of locations that each participant correctly recalled on a spatial memory test.

Researchers investigated whether a phone conversation reduces what drivers notice. They recruited 64 licensed drivers and randomly assigned each one to one of two conditions. Participants in one condition held a hands-free phone conversation while using a driving simulator. Participants in the other condition used the driving simulator without a phone. The researchers then recorded the number of road signs out of 30 that each participant failed to notice.

Read the summary of a hypothetical study, then answer parts A to F.

**Introduction.** Researchers investigated whether keeping a gratitude journal raises well-being. They hypothesized that the type of journal would affect subjective well-being.

**Participants.** The sample was 110 adult volunteers, recruited from one city. All participants gave informed consent, were told they could withdraw at any time, and were debriefed afterward. The plan was approved by an institutional review board.

**Method.** The participants were randomly assigned to one of two conditions. Participants in one condition wrote down three things they were grateful for every night for a month. Participants in the other condition wrote down three things they had done every night for a month. The researchers recorded each participant's rating of life satisfaction on a scale from 1 to 10 at the end of the month.

**Results.** The group that wrote about gratitude: mean life satisfaction (1 to 10) = 7.4. The group that wrote about daily events: mean life satisfaction (1 to 10) = 6.2. The difference was statistically significant (p = 0.01).

Use the three hypothetical sources to answer the question: **Why do people sometimes fail to help in an emergency?**

**Source A.** In an experiment, 80 students were randomly assigned to be alone or with four other people when smoke began to enter the room. Participants who were alone reported the smoke after a mean of 58 seconds; those in groups took a mean of 196 seconds (p = 0.01), and many never reported it.

**Source B.** In interviews after a staged emergency, participants who had not helped often said that they 'assumed someone else had already called for help' or that 'nobody else looked worried, so it could not be serious.'

**Source C.** Researchers observed 300 staged incidents in which a person dropped a bag of shopping in the street. Help was offered in 82 percent of incidents on quiet streets and in 41 percent of incidents on crowded streets.

questions.stem: A hormone released during childbirth and nursing strengthens the bond between parent and infant. Which hormone is this?

options.why: Melatonin is the hormone released by the pineal gland that makes a person sleepy.
Adrenaline is the hormone released by the adrenal glands that raises heart rate and energy during stress.
Correct. Oxytocin is the hormone that promotes bonding, trust and social attachment.
Leptin is the hormone released by fat cells that signals fullness and reduces hunger.

questions.explanation: Oxytocin is the hormone that promotes bonding, trust and social attachment.

questions.stem: A researcher destroys a tiny part of a rat's hypothalamus and observes how its eating changes. Which research technique is this?

options.why: An EEG is a recording of the electrical waves that sweep across the brain's surface.
A split brain is the condition in which the two hemispheres cannot communicate because the corpus callosum has been cut.
An fMRI is a scan that shows brain activity by tracking blood flow.
Correct. Lesioning is the destruction of a small area of brain tissue to study its function.

questions.explanation: Lesioning is the destruction of a small area of brain tissue to study its function.

questions.stem: Which of the following is best described as the giving and scoring of a test in the same way for everyone, and the comparison of scores with a pretested group?

options.why: Construct validity is the extent to which a test measures the concept it claims to measure.
Correct. Standardization is the giving and scoring of a test in the same way for everyone, and the comparison of scores with a pretested group.
Test-retest reliability is the consistency of scores when the same people take the same test twice.
Split-half reliability is the consistency of scores between two halves of the same test.

questions.explanation: Standardization is the giving and scoring of a test in the same way for everyone, and the comparison of scores with a pretested group.

questions.stem: Which of the following is best described as the ethical principle that psychologists must be honest and accurate?

options.why: Nonmaleficence is the ethical principle that psychologists must avoid doing harm.

options.text: Respect for people's rights and dignity
options.why: Respect for people's rights and dignity is the ethical principle that psychologists must protect privacy, confidentiality and the right of people to make their own choices.
Fidelity is the ethical principle that psychologists must be trustworthy and keep their professional promises.
Correct. Integrity is the ethical principle that psychologists must be honest and accurate.

questions.explanation: Integrity is the ethical principle that psychologists must be honest and accurate.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes epigenetics?

options.text: Research that compares identical and fraternal twins to estimate the influence of heredity
options.why: That describes a twin study.

options.text: Research that compares adopted children with their biological and adoptive relatives
options.why: That describes an adoption study.

options.text: The study of how the environment changes whether genes are expressed without changing the DNA itself
options.why: Correct. This is what epigenetics means.

options.text: The discredited movement that misused ideas about heredity to argue for selective breeding of humans
options.why: That describes eugenics.

questions.explanation: Epigenetics is the study of how the environment changes whether genes are expressed without changing the DNA itself.

questions.stem: After being rejected by a university, Hal says, 'I never really wanted to go there anyway; it is too far away.' Which defense mechanism is this?

options.why: Denial is the defense mechanism of refusing to accept a painful reality.
Projection is the defense mechanism of seeing one's own unacceptable impulses in other people.
Correct. Rationalization is the defense mechanism of giving a comfortable excuse in place of the real reason for a behavior.
Displacement is the defense mechanism of shifting an impulse from its real target to a safer one.

questions.explanation: Rationalization is the defense mechanism of giving a comfortable excuse in place of the real reason for a behavior.

questions.stem: Dee washes her hands forty times a day to relieve her worry. This repeated action is which of the following?

options.why: Correct. A compulsion is a repeated action that a person feels driven to perform to reduce anxiety.
Hoarding disorder is the disorder in which a person cannot throw away possessions, so that living spaces become cluttered.
Posttraumatic stress disorder is the disorder in which a person has flashbacks, nightmares, watchfulness and avoidance for more than a month after a terrifying event.
An obsession is an unwanted thought or urge that keeps returning and causes anxiety.

questions.explanation: A compulsion is a repeated action that a person feels driven to perform to reduce anxiety.

questions.stem: A drug produces a rush of pleasure by flooding the brain's reward pathway. Which neurotransmitter is most directly involved?

options.why: Glutamate is the brain's main excitatory neurotransmitter, which is involved in memory.
Norepinephrine is the neurotransmitter that helps control alertness and arousal.
Correct. Dopamine is the neurotransmitter that influences movement, attention, and feelings of reward.
GABA is the brain's main inhibitory neurotransmitter.

questions.explanation: Dopamine is the neurotransmitter that influences movement, attention, and feelings of reward.

questions.stem: Students are asked whether each word on a list is printed in capital letters. Which level of processing does this task use?

options.why: Correct. Structural encoding is the shallow encoding of a word based on its appearance.
Automatic processing is the encoding of information, such as space, time and frequency, without conscious effort.
Effortful processing is the encoding that requires attention and conscious effort.
Explicit memory is the memory of facts and experiences that a person can consciously recall and state.

questions.explanation: Structural encoding is the shallow encoding of a word based on its appearance.

questions.stem: A tourist calls another country's eating customs 'wrong' because they differ from the customs at home. This best illustrates which of the following?

options.why: An implicit attitude is an attitude that a person holds without being aware of it.
Correct. Ethnocentrism is the tendency to judge other cultures by the standards of one's own culture.
Discrimination is unjustified negative behavior toward a group and its members.
Prejudice is an unjustified negative attitude toward a group and its members.

questions.explanation: Ethnocentrism is the tendency to judge other cultures by the standards of one's own culture.

questions.stem: After being paid only one dollar to tell others that a boring task was fun, students came to believe the task really was enjoyable. Which concept best explains this change of attitude?

options.why: In-group bias is the tendency to favor the members of one's own group.
Out-group homogeneity bias is the tendency to see the members of other groups as all alike.
Correct. Cognitive dissonance is the discomfort a person feels when their actions and attitudes conflict, which motivates a change in one of them.
Confirmation bias is the tendency to search for and favor information that supports what one already believes.

questions.explanation: Cognitive dissonance is the discomfort a person feels when their actions and attitudes conflict, which motivates a change in one of them.

questions.stem: A researcher reports that the difference between two groups would occur by chance less than 5 times in 100. Which term describes this result?

options.why: A placebo is an inactive substance or treatment that looks like the real one.
A double-blind procedure is a procedure in which neither the participants nor the researchers who deal with them know who is in which condition.
Correct. Statistical significance is the conclusion that a result is unlikely to have occurred by chance, usually when p is below 0.05.
A confounding variable is a factor other than the independent variable that differs between groups and could explain the results.

questions.explanation: Statistical significance is the conclusion that a result is unlikely to have occurred by chance, usually when p is below 0.05.

questions.stem: Carl's behavior is far outside what people in his culture consider usual or acceptable. Which criterion for a psychological disorder does this meet?

options.why: Dysfunction is the criterion for a disorder that the behavior interferes with daily life, such as work and relationships.
Stigma is the negative attitudes and discrimination directed at people who have a psychological disorder.
The ICD is the World Health Organization's international system for classifying all diseases, including mental disorders.
Correct. Deviation from the social norm is the criterion for a disorder that the behavior differs markedly from what a culture expects.

questions.explanation: Deviation from the social norm is the criterion for a disorder that the behavior differs markedly from what a culture expects.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes random assignment?

options.text: The selecting of participants so that every member of the population has an equal chance of being chosen
options.why: That describes random sampling.

options.text: A sample made up of whoever is easiest for the researcher to reach
options.why: That describes a convenience sample.

options.text: The placing of participants in experimental conditions by chance
options.why: Correct. This is what random assignment means.

options.text: A flaw in selecting participants that makes the sample unlike the population
options.why: That describes sampling bias.

questions.explanation: Random assignment is the placing of participants in experimental conditions by chance.

questions.stem: Which part of the working memory model decides what to attend to and coordinates the sound and visual stores?

options.why: The visuospatial sketchpad is the part of working memory that briefly holds images and spatial information.
Correct. The central executive is the part of working memory that directs attention and coordinates the other parts.
The phonological loop is the part of working memory that briefly holds spoken and written words.
Long-term potentiation is the strengthening of the connections between neurons after repeated activation, which is the biological basis of memory.

questions.explanation: The central executive is the part of working memory that directs attention and coordinates the other parts.

questions.stem: A medication prevents the sending neuron from taking serotonin back, so more serotonin stays in the synapse. The medication is acting as which of the following?

options.why: Withdrawal is the unpleasant physical and psychological symptoms that follow stopping an addictive drug.
Correct. A reuptake inhibitor is a drug that keeps a neurotransmitter in the synapse longer by blocking its reabsorption.
Tolerance is the need for larger doses of a drug to get the same effect after repeated use.
An antagonist is a drug that decreases the action of a neurotransmitter, for example by blocking its receptors.

questions.explanation: A reuptake inhibitor is a drug that keeps a neurotransmitter in the synapse longer by blocking its reabsorption.

questions.stem: Which of the following is best described as the statistical method that finds clusters of related test items, used to identify basic traits?

options.why: Self-esteem is a person's overall feeling of self-worth.
Self-concept is all the thoughts and feelings a person has in answer to the question 'Who am I?'.
Reciprocal determinism is the idea that a person's behavior, thoughts and environment all influence one another.
Correct. Factor analysis is the statistical method that finds clusters of related test items, used to identify basic traits.

questions.explanation: Factor analysis is the statistical method that finds clusters of related test items, used to identify basic traits.

questions.stem: Why did the researchers assign the participants to the two conditions at random?

options.text: So that the study would have more participants
options.why: Random assignment does not change the sample size.

options.text: So that nobody would know the hypothesis
options.why: That describes a blind procedure.

options.text: So that the two groups would be similar at the start, and any difference could be attributed to the independent variable
options.why: Correct. Random assignment spreads individual differences evenly across the conditions.

options.text: So that the results could be generalized to the whole population
options.why: That is the purpose of random sampling, not random assignment.

questions.explanation: Random assignment spreads individual differences evenly across the conditions.

questions.stem: After a large, relaxed dinner, Ana's body directs energy toward digestion and her breathing slows. Which part of the nervous system is most active?

options.why: The autonomic nervous system is the division of the peripheral nervous system that controls glands and internal organs without conscious effort.
The central nervous system is the brain and spinal cord.
Correct. The parasympathetic nervous system is the division of the autonomic nervous system that calms the body and conserves energy.
The sympathetic nervous system is the division of the autonomic nervous system that arouses the body for fight or flight.

questions.explanation: The parasympathetic nervous system is the division of the autonomic nervous system that calms the body and conserves energy.

questions.stem: Another research team repeats this study with new subjects and obtains the same result. What is this called?

options.why: That is explaining the study to participants afterward.
That is an in-depth study of one individual.
Correct. Replication is repeating a study to see whether the finding holds.
That is how subjects are placed in conditions.

questions.explanation: Replication is repeating a study to see whether the finding holds.

questions.stem: Unsure which fork to use at a formal dinner, Sam watches the other guests and copies them, assuming they know. Which kind of influence is this?

options.why: A social norm is a rule for accepted and expected behavior in a group.
Correct. Informational social influence is the influence that comes from a person's willingness to accept others' views as evidence about reality.
The door-in-the-face technique is the strategy of making a large request that will be refused so that a smaller request is more likely to be accepted.
The halo effect is the tendency for one good quality of a person to make us assume they have other good qualities.

questions.explanation: Informational social influence is the influence that comes from a person's willingness to accept others' views as evidence about reality.

questions.stem: Which of the following is best described as the research method that measures two variables to see how they are related, without manipulating either?

options.why: Falsifiability is the quality of a claim that it could be shown to be wrong by evidence.
A hypothesis is a testable prediction about the relationship between variables.
Correct. A correlational study is the research method that measures two variables to see how they are related, without manipulating either.
A survey is the research method of collecting self-reported attitudes or behaviors from a sample by asking questions.

questions.explanation: A correlational study is the research method that measures two variables to see how they are related, without manipulating either.

questions.stem: Another research team repeats this study with new subjects and obtains the same result. What is this called?

options.why: That is an in-depth study of one individual.
That is explaining the study to participants afterward.
Correct. Replication is repeating a study to see whether the finding holds.
That is how subjects are placed in conditions.

questions.explanation: Replication is repeating a study to see whether the finding holds.

questions.stem: If the data were shown on a scatterplot, what pattern would the points form?

options.why: Only a correlation of +1.00 or −1.00 gives a perfect line.

options.text: A shapeless cloud with no slope
options.why: That would show a correlation near zero.

options.text: A loose band that slopes downward from left to right
options.why: That would show a negative correlation.

options.text: A loose band that slopes upward from left to right
options.why: Correct. A moderate positive correlation appears as a band of points sloping upward.

questions.explanation: A moderate positive correlation appears as a band of points sloping upward.

questions.stem: A cat in a puzzle box escapes faster on each trial because pressing the lever is followed by freedom and food. Which principle did Thorndike draw from this?

options.why: Correct. The law of effect is Thorndike's principle that behaviors followed by good outcomes become more likely and those followed by bad outcomes become less likely.
A secondary reinforcer is a reinforcer, such as money or praise, that gets its power through association with other rewards.
A primary reinforcer is a reinforcer, such as food or water, that satisfies a biological need and is rewarding without learning.
Superstitious behavior is a behavior that is repeated because it happened by chance just before a reward.

questions.explanation: The law of effect is Thorndike's principle that behaviors followed by good outcomes become more likely and those followed by bad outcomes become less likely.

questions.stem: A man has no memory of a frightening accident he was in as a child. In psychodynamic theory, which defense mechanism explains this?

options.why: Reaction formation is the defense mechanism of acting in the opposite way to one's unacceptable impulses.
Correct. Repression is the defense mechanism of pushing anxiety-arousing thoughts and memories out of awareness.
Regression is the defense mechanism of retreating to behavior from an earlier stage of development.
Sublimation is the defense mechanism of turning unacceptable impulses into socially valued activities.

questions.explanation: Repression is the defense mechanism of pushing anxiety-arousing thoughts and memories out of awareness.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the operational definition of the dependent variable?

options.why: This names the variable but does not say how it was measured.

options.text: The number of new puzzles out of ten that each child later solved without help
options.why: Correct. An operational definition states exactly how a variable is measured.

options.text: The random assignment of each one to a condition
options.why: This is a control procedure, not a definition of a variable.
This is the independent variable.

questions.explanation: An operational definition states exactly how a variable is measured.

questions.stem: Before taking part, each participant was told what the study would involve and what the risks were, and then agreed to take part. Which ethical guideline does this meet?

options.why: Confidentiality is keeping participants' data private.
Correct. Participants must agree to take part after being told what the study involves.
That is a research procedure, not an ethical guideline.
Debriefing happens after the study.

questions.explanation: Participants must agree to take part after being told what the study involves.

questions.stem: To work out 23 × 4 in her head, Elif holds the numbers in mind and manipulates them. Which memory system is she using?

options.why: Short-term memory is the memory store that briefly holds a few items, about seven, before they are stored or forgotten.
Long-term memory is the relatively permanent and limitless store of knowledge, skills and experiences.
Iconic memory is the brief sensory memory of a visual image, which lasts a few tenths of a second.
Correct. Working memory is the active processing of information held in mind, combining new input with knowledge from long-term memory.

questions.explanation: Working memory is the active processing of information held in mind, combining new input with knowledge from long-term memory.

questions.stem: When a crisis hits, Maria phones her friends, checks on her children and organizes the neighbors to help one another. Which response to stress is this?

options.why: Correct. The tend-and-befriend response is the response to stress of caring for others and seeking social support.
Health psychology is the field that studies how behavior, thoughts and emotions affect physical health and illness.
Eustress is the positive, motivating stress that comes from a challenge.
A stressor is an event or situation that a person sees as threatening or challenging.

questions.explanation: The tend-and-befriend response is the response to stress of caring for others and seeking social support.

questions.stem: Another research team repeats this study with new subjects and obtains the same result. What is this called?

options.why: That is how subjects are placed in conditions.
That is explaining the study to participants afterward.
Correct. Replication is repeating a study to see whether the finding holds.
That is an in-depth study of one individual.

questions.explanation: Replication is repeating a study to see whether the finding holds.

questions.stem: In the 1940s, surgeons cut the connections to patients' frontal lobes to calm them, often leaving them permanently listless. Which procedure was this?

options.why: Electroconvulsive therapy is the treatment for severe depression in which a brief electric current is passed through the brain of an anesthetized patient.
Transcranial magnetic stimulation is the treatment in which repeated magnetic pulses are applied to the surface of the brain to treat depression.
Correct. A lobotomy is the now-abandoned form of psychosurgery that cut the nerves connecting the frontal lobes to the rest of the brain.
Psychotropic medication is any drug that acts on the brain to treat the symptoms of a psychological disorder.

questions.explanation: A lobotomy is the now-abandoned form of psychosurgery that cut the nerves connecting the frontal lobes to the rest of the brain.

questions.stem: Taking a tablet makes Lena's headache go away, so she is more likely to take a tablet next time. This best illustrates which of the following?

options.why: Positive reinforcement is the strengthening of a behavior by adding a pleasant stimulus after it.
Correct. Negative reinforcement is the strengthening of a behavior by removing an unpleasant stimulus after it.
Negative punishment is the weakening of a behavior by removing a pleasant stimulus after it.
Positive punishment is the weakening of a behavior by adding an unpleasant stimulus after it.

questions.explanation: Negative reinforcement is the strengthening of a behavior by removing an unpleasant stimulus after it.

questions.stem: All of the subjects in this study were drawn from one group: 40 laboratory rats. What does this most limit?

options.text: Whether the study had a control group
options.why: The study had a comparison condition.

options.text: Whether the dependent variable was operationally defined
options.why: The measure was clearly defined.

options.text: How far the findings can be generalized to other populations
options.why: Correct. A sample that does not represent the wider population limits generalizability.

options.text: Whether a cause-and-effect conclusion can be drawn
options.why: Random assignment, not the sample, allows the causal conclusion.

questions.explanation: A sample that does not represent the wider population limits generalizability.

questions.stem: An eight-year-old answers the questions that a typical ten-year-old can answer. On Binet's test, ten is the child's what?

options.why: Correct. Mental age is the level of performance typical of a certain chronological age on an intelligence test.
Multiple intelligences is the theory that people have several independent kinds of intelligence, such as musical and interpersonal.
The intelligence quotient is originally, mental age divided by chronological age and multiplied by 100.
The Flynn effect is the steady rise in average intelligence test scores over the generations.

questions.explanation: Mental age is the level of performance typical of a certain chronological age on an intelligence test.

questions.stem: Seven students took a memory test. Their scores were 18, 1, 4, 7, 8, 11, 7. What is the mode of the scores?

options.why: Correct. The mode is the score that occurs most often.
That is the mean.
That is the range.
That is the highest score.

questions.explanation: In order, the scores are 1, 4, 7, 7, 8, 11, 18. The mode is the score that occurs most often. The one very high score pulls the mean (8) above the median (7), so the distribution is positively skewed.

questions.stem: After surviving a serious illness, Vera reports closer relationships, a greater appreciation of life and a new sense of purpose. This best illustrates which of the following?

options.why: Gratitude is the appreciation of the good things in one's life, the practice of which raises well-being.
Correct. Posttraumatic growth is the positive psychological change that some people experience after struggling with a very difficult event.
Subjective well-being is a person's own evaluation of how happy and satisfied they are with life.
Signature strengths is the positive character traits, such as kindness or curiosity, that are most central to a particular person.

questions.explanation: Posttraumatic growth is the positive psychological change that some people experience after struggling with a very difficult event.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the social responsibility norm?

options.text: Unselfish concern for the welfare of others
options.why: That describes altruism.

options.text: The physical and emotional exhaustion that results from long-term stress at work
options.why: That describes burnout.

options.text: The expectation that people will help those who have helped them
options.why: That describes the social reciprocity norm.

options.text: The expectation that people will help those who need help, even at a cost to themselves
options.why: Correct. This is what the social responsibility norm means.

questions.explanation: The social responsibility norm is the expectation that people will help those who need help, even at a cost to themselves.

questions.stem: After an argument with his roommate, Luis meditates and listens to music to settle his feelings. Which kind of coping is this?

options.why: Correct. Emotion-focused coping is the reducing of stress by managing one's emotional reaction rather than the stressor.
Problem-focused coping is the reducing of stress by changing the stressor itself or the way one deals with it.
Hypertension is persistently high blood pressure, which is made more likely by chronic stress.
Immune suppression is the weakening of the body's defenses against illness during long-term stress.

questions.explanation: Emotion-focused coping is the reducing of stress by managing one's emotional reaction rather than the stressor.

questions.stem: Which of the following is best described as study that is spread out over several sessions?

options.why: A hierarchy is the organizing of information into broad categories divided into narrower ones.
Massed practice is study that is crammed into one long session.
Correct. Distributed practice is study that is spread out over several sessions.
A mnemonic device is a memory aid that uses vivid images or organizing tricks.

questions.explanation: Distributed practice is study that is spread out over several sessions.

questions.stem: Can the researchers conclude that intelligence test score at age 11 causes a change in average school grade at age 16?

options.text: Yes, because the sample was large
options.why: A large sample does not turn a correlation into evidence of causation.

options.text: Yes, because the correlation is not zero
options.why: Any nonzero correlation still leaves the cause unknown.

options.text: No, because correlations can only be calculated in experiments
options.why: Correlations are calculated in non-experimental studies.

options.text: No, because a correlation does not show cause and effect
options.why: Correct. Without manipulating a variable and assigning subjects at random, other explanations cannot be ruled out.

questions.explanation: Without manipulating a variable and assigning subjects at random, other explanations cannot be ruled out.

questions.stem: Another research team repeats this study with new subjects and obtains the same result. What is this called?

options.why: That is explaining the study to participants afterward.
That is how subjects are placed in conditions.
Correct. Replication is repeating a study to see whether the finding holds.
That is an in-depth study of one individual.

questions.explanation: Replication is repeating a study to see whether the finding holds.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes obedience?

options.text: The cultural pattern that gives priority to the goals of the group and defines identity by group membership
options.why: That describes collectivism.

options.text: The adjusting of behavior or thinking to match a group standard
options.why: That describes conformity.

options.text: The following of the direct commands of an authority figure
options.why: Correct. This is what obedience means.

options.text: A situation in which people who each pursue their own interest end up harming everyone
options.why: That describes a social trap.

questions.explanation: Obedience is the following of the direct commands of an authority figure.

questions.stem: Which of the following is best described as a conflict in which a person must choose between two unattractive options?

options.why: Extrinsic motivation is the desire to do something to gain a reward or avoid a punishment.
An approach-avoidance conflict is a conflict in which one option has both attractive and unattractive features.
An approach-approach conflict is a conflict in which a person must choose between two attractive options.
Correct. An avoidance-avoidance conflict is a conflict in which a person must choose between two unattractive options.

questions.explanation: An avoidance-avoidance conflict is a conflict in which a person must choose between two unattractive options.

questions.stem: Which of the following would be a confounding variable in this study?

options.text: The two groups differed in anxiety at the end of the study
options.why: That is the dependent variable, the result being measured.

options.text: Each one was assigned to a condition at random
options.why: Random assignment reduces confounding; it is not a confound.

options.text: The drug group was also given weekly relaxation classes
options.why: Correct. It differs between the groups along with the independent variable, so it could explain the results instead.

options.text: One group differed from the other in the type of pill
options.why: That is the independent variable itself.

questions.explanation: It differs between the groups along with the independent variable, so it could explain the results instead.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes a longitudinal study?

options.text: The view that development is a gradual, steady process, like a ramp
options.why: That describes continuous development.

options.text: Research that follows the same people and retests them over a long period
options.why: Correct. This is what a longitudinal study means.

options.text: The developmental question of which traits stay the same through life and which ones alter
options.why: That describes stability and change.

options.text: The view that development happens in distinct stages, like a staircase
options.why: That describes discontinuous development.

questions.explanation: A longitudinal study is research that follows the same people and retests them over a long period.

questions.stem: Why did the researchers assign the children to the two conditions at random?

options.text: So that the two groups would be similar at the start, and any difference could be attributed to the independent variable
options.why: Correct. Random assignment spreads individual differences evenly across the conditions.

options.text: So that the results could be generalized to the whole population
options.why: That is the purpose of random sampling, not random assignment.

options.text: So that the study would have more participants
options.why: Random assignment does not change the sample size.

options.text: So that nobody would know the hypothesis
options.why: That describes a blind procedure.

questions.explanation: Random assignment spreads individual differences evenly across the conditions.

questions.stem: A four-year-old uses a banana as a telephone and 'calls' her grandmother. Which kind of play is this?

options.why: Correct. Pretend play is the play in which children act out imaginary roles and situations.
The personal fable is the belief of adolescents that they are unique and that bad things will not happen to them.
Emerging adulthood is the period from about 18 to the mid-twenties, between adolescence and full independence.
The social clock is a culture's preferred timing for life events such as marriage, parenthood and retirement.

questions.explanation: Pretend play is the play in which children act out imaginary roles and situations.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes a stimulant?

options.text: A drug, such as alcohol, that slows neural activity and body functions
options.why: That describes a depressant.

options.text: A drug, such as caffeine or cocaine, that speeds up neural activity and body functions
options.why: Correct. This is what a stimulant means.

options.text: A drug, such as heroin, that relieves pain by acting on endorphin receptors and is highly addictive
options.why: That describes an opioid.

options.text: A drug, such as marijuana, that distorts perception and can cause sensory experiences without sensory input
options.why: That describes a hallucinogen.

questions.explanation: A stimulant is a drug, such as caffeine or cocaine, that speeds up neural activity and body functions.

questions.stem: Immediately after hearing a shopping list, Ken can repeat the final three items but not the middle ones. This best illustrates which of the following?

options.why: The serial position effect is the tendency to remember the first and last items in a list better than the middle ones.
Correct. The recency effect is the tendency to remember the last items in a list well.
The primacy effect is the tendency to remember the first items in a list well.
The spacing effect is the finding that study spread over time produces better long-term memory than study crammed together.

questions.explanation: The recency effect is the tendency to remember the last items in a list well.

questions.stem: Which of the following is best described as the insecure attachment style in which a child seems indifferent when the caregiver leaves and ignores the caregiver on return?

options.why: Secure attachment is the attachment style in which a child uses the caregiver as a safe base, is upset when the caregiver leaves and is comforted on return.
Disorganized attachment is the insecure attachment style in which a child shows confused, contradictory behavior toward the caregiver.
Correct. Avoidant attachment is the insecure attachment style in which a child seems indifferent when the caregiver leaves and ignores the caregiver on return.
Separation anxiety is the distress that infants show when a familiar caregiver leaves, which peaks around 13 months.

questions.explanation: Avoidant attachment is the insecure attachment style in which a child seems indifferent when the caregiver leaves and ignores the caregiver on return.

questions.stem: If the data were shown on a scatterplot, what pattern would the points form?

options.text: A loose band that slopes upward from left to right
options.why: Correct. A moderate positive correlation appears as a band of points sloping upward.

options.text: A loose band that slopes downward from left to right
options.why: That would show a negative correlation.

options.text: A shapeless cloud with no slope
options.why: That would show a correlation near zero.
Only a correlation of +1.00 or −1.00 gives a perfect line.

questions.explanation: A moderate positive correlation appears as a band of points sloping upward.

questions.stem: A therapist says, 'It sounds as if you felt hurt when your friend did not call. Is that right?' Which technique is this?

options.why: Group therapy is the therapy in which several clients meet together with a therapist and benefit from each other's support.
Hypnosis is a state of heightened suggestibility that can help reduce pain and anxiety but does not reliably recover memories.
Correct. Active listening is the technique of echoing, restating and seeking clarification of what the client says.
Person-centered therapy is the humanistic therapy in which the therapist provides acceptance and empathy so that the client can grow.

questions.explanation: Active listening is the technique of echoing, restating and seeking clarification of what the client says.

questions.stem: Which of the following is best described as the disorder in which a person has an intense fear of being judged or embarrassed in social situations?

options.why: Ataque de nervios is the culture-bound anxiety syndrome, found mainly among people of Caribbean descent, marked by shouting, crying and a feeling of being out of control.
A specific phobia is the disorder in which a person has an intense, irrational fear of a particular object or situation.
Correct. Social anxiety disorder is the disorder in which a person has an intense fear of being judged or embarrassed in social situations.
Panic disorder is the disorder in which a person has repeated, unexpected episodes of intense fear with physical symptoms such as chest pain.

questions.explanation: Social anxiety disorder is the disorder in which a person has an intense fear of being judged or embarrassed in social situations.

questions.stem: Can the researchers conclude that resting heart rate causes a change in self-rated anxiety?

options.text: Yes, because the correlation is not zero
options.why: Any nonzero correlation still leaves the cause unknown.

options.text: No, because a correlation does not show cause and effect
options.why: Correct. Without manipulating a variable and assigning subjects at random, other explanations cannot be ruled out.

options.text: Yes, because the sample was large
options.why: A large sample does not turn a correlation into evidence of causation.

options.text: No, because correlations can only be calculated in experiments
options.why: Correlations are calculated in non-experimental studies.

questions.explanation: Without manipulating a variable and assigning subjects at random, other explanations cannot be ruled out.

questions.stem: After failing a quiz, Ty says, 'I am just not a math person,' and stops trying. Which belief does this show?

options.why: Correct. A fixed mindset is the belief that intelligence is set and cannot be changed.
Stereotype lift is the boost in performance that comes from awareness that another group is negatively stereotyped.
A growth mindset is the belief that intelligence can be developed through effort and learning.
An aptitude test is a test that predicts a person's ability to learn or perform in the future.

questions.explanation: A fixed mindset is the belief that intelligence is set and cannot be changed.

questions.stem: Which of the following is best described as the way the wording of an issue affects decisions and judgments?

options.why: The representativeness heuristic is the judging of how likely something is by how well it matches a prototype, while ignoring base rates.
Priming is the activation, often without awareness, of certain associations that then influence perception or behavior.
The sunk-cost fallacy is the tendency to keep investing in something because of what has already been spent on it.
Correct. Framing is the way the wording of an issue affects decisions and judgments.

questions.explanation: Framing is the way the wording of an issue affects decisions and judgments.

questions.stem: Mr. Diaz snores loudly, stops breathing many times each night, and feels exhausted during the day. Which sleep disorder does he most likely have?

options.why: Correct. Sleep apnea is a sleep disorder in which breathing repeatedly stops during sleep, causing brief awakenings.
Insomnia is a sleep disorder with ongoing difficulty falling asleep or staying asleep.
REM sleep behavior disorder is a sleep disorder in which the normal paralysis of REM sleep is missing, so the person acts out dreams.
Narcolepsy is a sleep disorder with sudden, uncontrollable attacks of sleep, often straight into REM sleep.

questions.explanation: Sleep apnea is a sleep disorder in which breathing repeatedly stops during sleep, causing brief awakenings.

questions.stem: Humanistic psychologists argue that people are naturally motivated to become the best version of themselves. What is this motivation called?

options.why: Correct. The self-actualizing tendency is in humanistic theory, the inborn drive of people to grow and fulfill their potential.
Unconditional positive regard is the attitude of total acceptance toward another person, whatever they say or do.
A projective test is a personality test, such as an inkblot test, that asks people to interpret unclear images in order to reveal hidden feelings.
A defense mechanism is in psychodynamic theory, a method the ego uses without awareness to reduce anxiety by distorting reality.

questions.explanation: The self-actualizing tendency is in humanistic theory, the inborn drive of people to grow and fulfill their potential.

questions.stem: Carl avoided fish after becoming ill only once. Learning that takes place after a single pairing is called which of the following?

options.why: A taste aversion is a learned dislike of a food that was followed by illness.
Habituation is the decrease in response to a stimulus that is presented over and over.
Correct. One-trial conditioning is learning that happens after a single pairing of two stimuli.
Biological preparedness is the inborn readiness to learn some associations, such as taste and nausea, more easily than others.

questions.explanation: One-trial conditioning is learning that happens after a single pairing of two stimuli.

questions.stem: If the data were shown on a scatterplot, what pattern would the points form?

options.text: A loose band that slopes downward from left to right
options.why: That would show a negative correlation.

options.text: A shapeless cloud with no slope
options.why: That would show a correlation near zero.

options.text: A loose band that slopes upward from left to right
options.why: Correct. A moderate positive correlation appears as a band of points sloping upward.
Only a correlation of +1.00 or −1.00 gives a perfect line.

questions.explanation: A moderate positive correlation appears as a band of points sloping upward.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes reversibility?

options.text: The understanding that quantity stays the same when shape or arrangement changes
options.why: That describes conservation.

options.text: The understanding that an action can be undone to return things to their original state
options.why: Correct. This is what reversibility means.

options.text: The difficulty that young children have in taking another person's point of view
options.why: That describes egocentrism.

options.text: The belief of young children that lifeless objects have feelings and intentions
options.why: That describes animism.

questions.explanation: Reversibility is the understanding that an action can be undone to return things to their original state.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the broaden-and-build theory?

options.text: The basic emotions, such as happiness, sadness, fear and anger, whose facial expressions are recognized across cultures
options.why: That describes universal emotions.

options.text: The idea that the expression on a person's face can influence the emotion the person feels
options.why: That describes the facial-feedback hypothesis.

options.text: The theory that positive emotions widen a person's awareness and help build lasting skills and resources
options.why: Correct. This is what the broaden-and-build theory means.

options.text: The interpretation of a situation, which shapes the emotion a person feels
options.why: That describes cognitive appraisal.

questions.explanation: The broaden-and-build theory is the theory that positive emotions widen a person's awareness and help build lasting skills and resources.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes an eclectic approach?

options.text: The presence of two or more disorders in the same person at the same time
options.why: That describes comorbidity.

options.text: The view that disorders result from the interaction of biological, psychological and social factors
options.why: That describes the biopsychosocial model.

options.text: The view that a disorder develops when an inherited vulnerability is triggered by stressful experience
options.why: That describes the diathesis-stress model.

options.text: The use of techniques from several types of therapy, depending on the client's problem
options.why: Correct. This is what an eclectic approach means.

questions.explanation: An eclectic approach is the use of techniques from several types of therapy, depending on the client's problem.

questions.stem: Four studies of child development report these correlation coefficients: +0.52, −0.93, +0.20, +0.12. Which coefficient shows the weakest relationship?

options.why: Correct. Strength is the distance from zero, whatever the sign; +0.12 is closest to zero.
+0.20 is farther from zero.
+0.52 is farther from zero.
−0.93 is farther from zero.

questions.explanation: The sign of a correlation shows its direction; its distance from zero shows its strength. +0.12 is closest to zero.

questions.stem: Which of the following is best described as the confrontational cognitive therapy, developed by Ellis, that actively challenges a client's irrational beliefs?

options.why: The cognitive triad is the pattern of negative thoughts about oneself, the world and the future that is found in depression.
Correct. Rational emotive behavior therapy is the confrontational cognitive therapy, developed by Ellis, that actively challenges a client's irrational beliefs.
Dialectical behavior therapy is the therapy that teaches skills for tolerating distress and controlling emotions, often used for borderline personality disorder.
Cognitive restructuring is the technique of identifying irrational thoughts and replacing them with more realistic ones.

questions.explanation: Rational emotive behavior therapy is the confrontational cognitive therapy, developed by Ellis, that actively challenges a client's irrational beliefs.

questions.stem: With a blocked nose, Jo finds that her favorite food has almost no flavor. This best illustrates which of the following?

options.why: The absolute threshold is the weakest level of a stimulus that a person can detect half of the time.
Correct. Sensory interaction is the way one sense influences another, as when smell affects taste.
Sensory adaptation is the reduced sensitivity that follows constant, unchanging stimulation.
The just-noticeable difference is the smallest difference between two stimuli that a person can detect half of the time.

questions.explanation: Sensory interaction is the way one sense influences another, as when smell affects taste.

questions.stem: A two-year-old insists, 'Me do it!' when getting dressed. Which of Erikson's stages is this?

options.why: Correct. Autonomy versus shame and doubt is Erikson's stage in toddlerhood, in which children learn to do things for themselves.
Trust versus mistrust is Erikson's stage in infancy, in which babies learn whether their needs will be met.
Industry versus inferiority is Erikson's stage in elementary school, in which children learn to feel competent or else feel inadequate.
Initiative versus guilt is Erikson's stage in the preschool years, in which children learn to start tasks and carry out plans.

questions.explanation: Autonomy versus shame and doubt is Erikson's stage in toddlerhood, in which children learn to do things for themselves.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes a fear hierarchy?

options.text: The exposure therapy that pairs relaxation with a graded series of anxiety-arousing stimuli
options.why: That describes systematic desensitization.

options.text: The behavioral treatment that pairs an unwanted behavior with an unpleasant stimulus
options.why: That describes aversion therapy.

options.text: A list of feared situations arranged from the least to the most frightening
options.why: Correct. This is what a fear hierarchy means.

options.text: The use of the principles of conditioning to increase helpful behaviors and reduce harmful ones
options.why: That describes applied behavior analysis.

questions.explanation: A fear hierarchy is a list of feared situations arranged from the least to the most frightening.

questions.stem: Why did the researchers assign the participants to the two conditions at random?

options.text: So that the results could be generalized to the whole population
options.why: That is the purpose of random sampling, not random assignment.

options.text: So that the study would have more participants
options.why: Random assignment does not change the sample size.

options.text: So that the two groups would be similar at the start, and any difference could be attributed to the independent variable
options.why: Correct. Random assignment spreads individual differences evenly across the conditions.

options.text: So that nobody would know the hypothesis
options.why: That describes a blind procedure.

questions.explanation: Random assignment spreads individual differences evenly across the conditions.

questions.stem: In a town where most people earn modest incomes and a few earn millions, the mean income is far above the median. Which shape does the distribution have?

options.why: The range is the difference between the highest and lowest scores.
The mode is the score that occurs most often.
The standard deviation is the measure of how much scores vary around the mean.
Correct. A positive skew is a distribution with a few extremely high scores, which pull the mean above the median.

questions.explanation: A positive skew is a distribution with a few extremely high scores, which pull the mean above the median.

questions.stem: A child cannot solve a puzzle alone but can solve it with a few hints from a teacher. In Vygotsky's theory, this puzzle falls within which of the following?

options.why: Fluid intelligence is the ability to reason quickly and abstractly, which tends to decline in older adulthood.
Correct. The zone of proximal development is the gap between what a learner can do alone and what the learner can do with help.
Crystallized intelligence is the accumulated knowledge and verbal skills that tend to increase with age.
Dementia is a serious decline in memory and thinking that interferes with daily life, most common in old age.

questions.explanation: The zone of proximal development is the gap between what a learner can do alone and what the learner can do with help.

questions.stem: What is the dependent variable in this study?

options.why: This was manipulated by the researchers: it is the independent variable.

options.text: The condition to which each one was assigned
options.why: This describes the independent variable.
A hypothesis is a prediction, not a variable.
Correct. The dependent variable is the outcome that the researchers measured.

questions.explanation: The dependent variable is the outcome that the researchers measured.

questions.stem: Scores on a test are normally distributed with a mean of 100 and a standard deviation of 15. About what percentage of scores are between 85 and 115?

options.why: This does not match the 68–95 rule for a normal distribution.
This does not match the 68–95 rule for a normal distribution.
This does not match the 68–95 rule for a normal distribution.
Correct. About 68% of scores fall within one standard deviation of the mean.

questions.explanation: About 68% of scores fall within one standard deviation of the mean. (85 and 115 are one standard deviation from the mean; 70 and 130 are two.)

questions.stem: Which group served as the control group?

options.why: Only the comparison group is the control group.

options.text: The group that drove without a phone
options.why: Correct. The control group is the comparison group that does not receive the treatment being tested.

options.text: Neither group, because the study had no comparison condition
options.why: The second condition is the comparison.

options.text: The group that talked on the phone
options.why: This group received the treatment being tested: it is the experimental group.

questions.explanation: The control group is the comparison group that does not receive the treatment being tested.

questions.title: Article analysis: a study of subjective well-being

parts.prompt: Identify the research method used in the study.

rubric.criterion: Identifies the method as an experiment.
rubric.example: The study is an experiment: the researchers manipulated a variable and randomly assigned the subjects to conditions.

parts.prompt: State the operational definition of subjective well-being.

rubric.criterion: States how the variable was measured in this study.
rubric.example: Subjective well-being was defined as each participant's rating of life satisfaction on a scale from 1 to 10 at the end of the month.

parts.prompt: Describe the meaning of the difference between the two group averages.

rubric.criterion: Accurately describes which group scored higher or lower and what that means for the variable measured.
rubric.example: The gratitude group reported higher life satisfaction. On average, the value was 7.4 for the group that wrote about gratitude and 6.2 for the group that wrote about daily events, and a p value of 0.01 means a difference this large is unlikely to be due to chance.

parts.prompt: Identify at least one ethical guideline applied by the researchers.

rubric.criterion: Identifies an ethical guideline that the summary shows was followed.
rubric.example: Informed consent: participants agreed to take part after being told about the study. (Also acceptable: debriefing; the right to withdraw; approval by an institutional review board.)

parts.prompt: Explain the extent to which the research findings may or may not be generalizable, using specific and relevant evidence from the study.

rubric.criterion: Explains a limit (or strength) of generalizability with reference to the sample.
rubric.example: The sample was 110 adult volunteers from one city, so the findings may not apply to people of other ages, cultures or backgrounds. Because the sample was not randomly selected from a wider population, it may not be representative.

parts.prompt: Explain how at least one of the research findings supports or refutes the researchers' hypothesis.

rubric.criterion: Uses a specific finding from the study as evidence.
rubric.example: The gratitude group reported higher life satisfaction. (7.4 compared with 6.2).

rubric.criterion: Explains how the finding supports the hypothesis, using a psychological concept.
rubric.example: This supports the hypothesis that the type of journal affects subjective well-being. Because subjects were randomly assigned, the difference can be attributed to the type of journal. The finding illustrates positive psychology: practicing gratitude increases subjective well-being.

questions.title: Evidence-based question: Why do people sometimes fail to help in an emergency?

parts.prompt: Propose a specific and defensible claim, based in psychological science, that responds to the question.

rubric.criterion: States a claim that answers the question and can be supported by the sources.
rubric.example: People are less likely to help when others are present, because each person feels less responsible and looks to others to decide how to act.

parts.prompt: (i) Support your claim using at least one piece of specific and relevant evidence from one of the sources. (ii) Explain how the evidence supports your claim, using a psychological perspective, theory, concept or research finding learned in AP Psychology.

rubric.criterion: Uses specific, relevant evidence from one source and names the source.
rubric.example: In Source A, participants who were alone reported smoke after 58 seconds, but those in groups of five took 196 seconds.

rubric.criterion: Explains how the evidence supports the claim.
rubric.example: This supports the claim through the bystander effect and diffusion of responsibility: when others are present, each person feels less personal responsibility to act.

rubric.criterion: Correctly applies a psychological concept in the explanation.
rubric.example: The concept must be named and applied correctly, as in the model explanation.

parts.prompt: (i) Support your claim using an additional piece of specific and relevant evidence from a different source. (ii) Explain how this evidence supports your claim, using a different psychological perspective, theory, concept or research finding.

rubric.criterion: Uses specific, relevant evidence from a different source and names the source.
rubric.example: In Source B, participants said that 'nobody else looked worried, so it could not be serious.'

rubric.criterion: Explains how the evidence supports the claim.
rubric.example: This supports the claim through informational social influence: in an unclear situation, people use the behavior of others as evidence of what is happening, so if nobody reacts, each person concludes there is no emergency.

rubric.criterion: Correctly applies a different psychological concept from the one used in part B.
rubric.example: The concept must differ from the one used in part B and be applied correctly.
